beats.text: She was held at knifepoint. And felt no fear.
She is known only as S. M. A rare disease destroyed a tiny part of her brain, on both sides: the amygdala.
Researchers took her to a haunted house. She laughed, and poked a monster in the head.
In a pet store, she kept asking to touch the snakes.
Then they had her breathe air with extra carbon dioxide. And she panicked. A feeling she said was completely new.
Fear of the world outside needs the amygdala. Fear from inside your own body doesn't.
So fear isn't one thing. It's at least two.

sources: Feinstein, Adolphs, Damasio & Tranel (2011). The human amygdala and the induction and experience of fear. Current Biology 21(1). Patient S.M., Urbach-Wiethe disease, bilateral amygdala damage; no fear at Waverly Hills haunted house (laughed, poked a monster's head), wanted to touch snakes in exotic pet store, horror clips; held at knife- and gunpoint without fear. Via Science News.

Feinstein et al. (2013). Fear and panic in humans with bilateral amygdala damage. Nature Neuroscience 16(3). CO2 inhalation triggered panic in S.M., A.M., B.G.; S.M. described it as new, 'number one, worst' feeling. Via BPS Research Digest.
